The '''Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited''' ('''ONGC''') is an Indian [[Public Sector Undertakings in India|central public sector undertaking]] which is the largest government-owned oil and gas explorer and producer in the country. It accounts for around 70 per cent of India's domestic production of [[petroleum|crude oil]] and around 84 per cent of [[natural gas]]. Headquartered in [[Delhi]], ONGC is under the [[ownership]] of the [[Government of India]] and administration of [[Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas]]. It was founded on 14 August 1956 by the Government of India. In November 2010, the Government of India conferred the ''[[Public sector undertakings in India|Maharatna]]'' status to ONGC.

In a survey by the Government of India for fiscal year 2019–20, it was ranked as the largest profit making [[Public sector undertakings in India|central public sector undertaking]] (PSU) in India. It is ranked 5th among the Top 250 Global Energy Companies by [[Platts]].

ONGC is [[vertical integration|vertically integrated]] across the entire oil and gas industry. It is involved in exploring for and exploiting [[hydrocarbon]]s in 26 [[sedimentary basin]]s of India, owns and operates over 11,000 [[kilometer]]s of [[Pipelines in India|pipelines]] in the country and operates a total of around 230 drilling and workover rigs. Its international subsidiary ONGC Videsh currently has projects in 15 countries. ONGC has discovered seven out of the eight producing Indian basins, adding over 7.15 billion [[tonne]]s of In-place Oil & Gas volume of hydrocarbons in Indian basins. Against a global decline of production from matured fields, ONGC has maintained production from its brownfields like [[Mumbai High Field|Mumbai High]], with the help of aggressive investments in various IOR (improved oil recovery) and EOR ([[Enhanced Oil Recovery]]) schemes. ONGC has many matured fields with a current recovery factor of 25–33%.<ref name="AR201213">{{cite web|url=http://www.ongcindia.com/wps/wcm/OngcHTML/Annual_Report_2012_13/Annual_Report_2012_13.pdf|title=Annual Report 2012-13|publisher=ONGC|date=29 May 2013|access-date=9 November 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109152410/http://www.ongcindia.com/wps/wcm/OngcHTML/Annual_Report_2012_13/Annual_Report_2012_13.pdf|archive-date=9 November 2013|url-status=live}}</ref> Its Reserve Replacement Ratio for between 2005 and 2013, has been more than one.<ref name="AR201213" />

During FY 2012–13, ONGC had to share the highest ever under-recovery of {{INRConvert|89.77|t|lk=r|mode=historical|year=2013}} (an increase of {{INRConvert|17.89|b|lk=r|mode=historical|year=2013}} over the previous financial year) towards the under-recoveries of Oil Marketing Companies ([[Indian Oil Corporation|IOC]], [[Bharat Petroleum|BPCL]] and [[Hindustan Petroleum|HPCL]]).<ref name="AR201213" />

On 1 November 2017, the [[Union Council of Ministers|Union Cabinet]] approved ONGC for acquiring a majority 51.11% stake in [[Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited]] (HPCL).<ref>{{Cite news |date=20 January 2018 |title=ONGC buys government's 51.11% stake in HPCL for Rs 36,915 crore |work=[[The Times of India]] |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/ongc-buys-govts-51-11-stake-in-hpcl-for-rs-36915-crore/articleshow/62582328.cms |access-date=15 April 2023 |issn=0971-8257 |archive-date=25 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230425182555/https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/ongc-buys-govts-51-11-stake-in-hpcl-for-rs-36915-crore/articleshow/62582328.cms |url-status=live }}</ref> On 30 January 2018, ONGC completed the acquisition of 51.11% stake in HPCL.<ref>{{Cite web |date=8 January 2020 |title=ONGC: An acquisition thrust by govt way too costly |url=https://www.deccanherald.com/business/business-news/ongc-an-acquisition-thrust-by-govt-way-too-costly-792336.html |access-date=15 April 2023 |website=[[Deccan Herald]] |language=en |archive-date=15 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230415071832/https://www.deccanherald.com/business/business-news/ongc-an-acquisition-thrust-by-govt-way-too-costly-792336.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

==History==

===Foundation to 1956===
[[File:Pumpjack in Sivasagar.jpg|right|thumb|Pumpjack working in an oilfield of ONGC at Sivasagar, Assam]]
Before the independence of India in 1947, the [[Assam oil|Assam Oil Company]] in the north-eastern and [[Attock Oil Company]] in the north-western part of the [[Akhand Bharat|undivided India]] were the only oil-producing companies, with minimal exploration input. The major part of Indian sedimentary basins was deemed to be unfit for the development of oil and gas resources.<ref name=History>{{cite web |url=http://www.ongcindia.com/wps/wcm/connect/ongcindia/Home/Company/History/ |title=History |publisher=ONGC |access-date=10 November 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109195336/http://www.ongcindia.com/wps/wcm/connect/ongcindia/Home/Company/History/ |archive-date=9 November 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref>

After independence, the Central Government of India realized the importance of [[Fossil fuel|oil and gas]] for rapid industrial development and its strategic role in defence. Consequently, while framing the Industrial Policy Statement of 1948, the development of the petroleum industry in the country was considered to be of utmost necessity.<ref name=History/>

Until 1955, private oil companies mainly carried out exploration of hydrocarbon resources of India. In [[Assam]], the Assam Oil Company was producing oil at [[Digboi Refinery|Digboi]] (discovered in 1889) and Oil India Ltd. (a 50% joint venture between Government of India and Burmah Oil Company) was engaged in developing two newly discovered large fields [[Naharkatiya]] and [[Moran Town|Moraan]] in Assam. In [[West Bengal]], the Indo-Stanvac Petroleum project (a joint venture between [[Government of India|the Government of India]] and [[Standard Vacuum Oil Company]] of USA) was engaged in exploration work. The vast sedimentary tract in other parts of India and adjoining offshore remained largely unexplored.<ref name=History/>

In 1955, the Government of India decided to develop the oil and natural gas resources in the various regions of the country as part of the public sector development. With this objective, an Oil and Natural Gas Directorate was set up towards the end of 1955, as a subordinate office under the then Ministry of Natural Resources and Scientific Research. The department was constituted with a nucleus of geoscientists from the [[Geological Survey of India]].<ref name=History/>

A delegation under the leadership of the minister of Natural Resources visited several European countries to study the status of the oil industry in those countries and to facilitate the training of Indian professionals for exploring potential oil and gas reserves. Experts from [[Romania]], the [[Soviet Union]], the [[United States]] and [[West Germany]] subsequently visited India and helped the government with their expertise. [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] experts later drew up a detailed plan for [[geological]] and [[geophysical]] surveys and drilling operations to be carried out in the 2nd [[Five-Year plans of India|Five Year Plan (1956–61)]].<ref name=History/>

In April 1956, the Government of India adopted the [[Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956|Industrial Policy Resolution]], which placed Mineral Oil Industry among the schedule 'A' industries, the future development of which was to be the sole and exclusive responsibility of the state.<ref name=History/>

Soon, after the formation of the Oil and Natural Gas Directorate, it became apparent that it would not be possible for the Directorate with its limited financial and administrative powers as a subordinate office of the Government, to function efficiently. So in August 1956, the Directorate was raised to the status of a commission with enhanced powers, although it continued to be under the government. In October 1959, the commission was converted into a statutory body by an act of the Indian Parliament, which enhanced powers of the commission further. The main functions of the Oil and Natural Gas Commission subject to the provisions of the Act were "to plan, promote, organize and implement programs for development of Petroleum Resources and the production and sale of petroleum and petroleum products produced by it, and to perform such other functions as the Central Government may, from time to time, assign to it ". The act further outlined the activities and steps to be taken by ONGC in fulfilling its mandate.<ref name=History/>

===1961 to 2000===
[[File:ONGC Oil Platform.jpg|thumb|right|An ONGC platform at [[Bombay High]] in the [[Arabian Sea]]]]

Since its inception, ONGC has been instrumental in transforming the country's limited upstream sector into a large viable playing field, with its activities spread throughout India and significantly in overseas territories. In the inland areas, ONGC not only found new resources in Assam but also established new oil province in Cambay basin (Gujarat), while adding new petroliferous areas in the Assam-Arakan Fold Belt and East coast basins (both onshore and offshore).<ref name=History/>

In 1963, ONGC discovered oil and gas sites in [[Sivasagar district]] and established oilfields in Lakua, Gelekey, and Rudrasagar.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Barbora |first1=Sanjay |last2=Phukan |first2=Sarat |date=5 April 2022 |title=Mines, plantations, and militarisation: Environmental conflicts in Tinsukia, Assam |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/25148486221089820 |journal=Environment and Planning E: Nature and Space |volume=6 |language=en |pages=222–239 |doi=10.1177/25148486221089820 |s2cid=248016289 |issn=2514-8486 |access-date=10 April 2022 |archive-date=9 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220409145830/https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/25148486221089820 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

ONGC went offshore in the early 1970s and discovered a giant oil field in the form of [[Bombay High]], now known as Mumbai High. This discovery, along with subsequent discoveries of huge oil and gas fields in Western offshore changed the oil scenario of the country. Subsequently, over 5 billion tonnes of hydrocarbons, which were present in the country, were discovered. The most important contribution of ONGC, however, is its self-reliance and development of core competence in E&P activities at a globally competitive level.<ref name="History" />

ONGC became a public listed company in February 1994,<ref name=":0" /> with 20% of its equity were sold to the public and eighty per cent retained by the Indian government. At the time, ONGC employed 48,000 people and had reserves and surpluses worth {{INRConvert|104.34|b|year=1994}}, in addition to its intangible assets. The corporation's net worth of {{INRConvert|107.77|b|mode=historical|year=1994}} was the largest of any Indian company.{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}}

In 1958 the then chairman, Keshav Dev Malaviya, held a meeting with some geologists in the Mussoorie office of the Geology Directorate where he accepted the need for ONGC to go outside India too in order to enhance Indian owned capacity for oil production. The argument in support for this step, by LP Mathur and BS Negi, was that Indian demand for crude would go up at a faster rate than discoveries by ONGC in India.{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}}

Malaviya followed this up by making ONGC apply for exploration licences in the Persian Gulf. Iran gave ONGC four blocks and Malaviya visited Milan and Bartlesville, Oklahoma to request ENI and Phillips Petroleum to join as partners in the Iran venture. This resulted in the discovery of the Rostum oilfield in the early 'sixties, very soon after the discovery of Ankleshwar in Gujarat. This was the very first investment by the Indian public sector in foreign countries and oil from Rostum and Raksh was brought to Cochin where it was refined in a refinery built with technical assistance from Phillips.{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}}

===2001 to present===
In 2003, ONGC Videsh Limited (OVL), the division of ONGC concerned with its foreign assets, acquired [[Talisman Energy]]'s 25% stake in the Greater Nile Oil project.<ref name=GT-DEX-2003-CN-MP-I>{{cite news|title=Talisman pulls out of Sudan|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/2835713.stm|publisher=BBC News|access-date=4 May 2012|agency=Associated Press|date=10 March 2003|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121112081754/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/2835713.stm|archive-date=12 November 2012|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2006, a commemorative coin set was issued to mark the 50th anniversary of the founding of ONGC, making it only the second Indian company ([[State Bank of India]] being the first) to have such a coin issued in its honour.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://numismaticscollections.blogspot.com/p/50-years-of-ongc.html |title=2006 - 50 Years of ONGC |publisher=Numismatics Collection |access-date=3 September 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://numismaticscollections.blogspot.com/p/commemorative-coins-index.html |title=Commemorative Coins Index |publisher=Numismatics Collection |access-date=3 September 2024}}</ref>

In 2011, ONGC applied to purchase 2000 acres of land at [[Dahanu]] to process offshore gas.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://articles.timesofindia.indiatimes.com/2011-09-10/mumbai/30138777_1_processing-plant-dahanu-gas-block|title=ONGC seeks 2K acres govt land at Dahanu|agency=[[Times News Network]]|last=Lewis|first=Clara|date=11 September 2011|access-date=13 September 2011|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120713023406/http://articles.timesofindia.indiatimes.com/2011-09-10/mumbai/30138777_1_processing-plant-dahanu-gas-block|archive-date=13 July 2012|work=[[The Times of India]]|url-status=dead}}</ref> ONGC Videsh, along with Statoil ASA ([[Norway]]) and Repsol SA ([[Spain]]), has been engaged in deep-water drilling off the northern coast of Cuba in 2012.<ref>Oil and Gas Journal 22 May 2012 [http://www.ogj.com/articles/2012/05/repsol-declares-cuba-deepwater-wildcat-dry.html Repsol declares Cuba deepwater wildcat dry]. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150920030625/http://www.ogj.com/articles/2012/05/repsol-declares-cuba-deepwater-wildcat-dry.html |date=20 September 2015 }}</ref> On 11 August 2012, ONGC announced that it had made a large oil discovery in the D1 oilfield off the west coast of India, which will help it to raise the output of the field from around 12,500 barrels per day (bpd) to a peak output of 60,000 bpd.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://zeenews.india.com/business/news/companies/ongc-makes-huge-oil-discovery-off-west-coast_57871.html|title= ONGC makes huge oil discovery off West coast|date= 12 August 2012|access-date= 12 August 2012|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120817135250/http://zeenews.india.com/business/news/companies/ongc-makes-huge-oil-discovery-off-west-coast_57871.html|archive-date= 17 August 2012|url-status= live}}</ref>

In February 2016, the board of ONGC approved an investment of {{INRConvert|50.5|b|mode=historical|year=2016}} in [[Tripura]] for drilling of wells and creation of surface facilities to produce 5.1 million standard cubic feet per day gas from the state's fields.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.thehindubusinessline.com/companies/ongc-board-approves-rs-5050cr-investment-in-tripura/article8261921.ece | title=ONGC board approves Rs. 5,050-cr investment in Tripura | work=The Hindu | date=20 February 2016 | agency=PTI | access-date=21 February 2016 | location=Agartala | archive-date=16 September 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210916163917/https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/companies/ongc-board-approves-rs-5050cr-investment-in-tripura/article8261921.ece | url-status=live }}</ref>

On 19 July 2017, the Government of India approved the acquisition of [[Hindustan Petroleum Corporation]] by ONGC.<ref>{{Cite web| url=http://www.hindustantimes.com/business-news/cabinet-allows-ongc-to-buy-out-govt-stake-in-refiner-hpcl/story-2oqzKRbSfScBDmCt3oiL2L.html| title=Cabinet allows ONGC to buy out govt stake in refiner HPCL| date=19 July 2017| access-date=19 July 2017}}</ref>

According to reports, ONGC's oil production decreased from 20.80 million tonnes in the fiscal year 2018 to 16.88 million tonnes during the April–February period of the fiscal year 2022–23.<ref name=":1" />

In the year 2023, ONGC made an announcement stating its plans to invest a large sum of money in the exploration of deepwater and ultra-deepwater, despite the ongoing decrease in the company's production of oil and gas.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=ONGC shares as investors book profits after sharp gains |url=https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/business/stocks/ongc-shares-as-investors-book-profits-after-sharp-gains-10399651.html |access-date=15 April 2023 |website=Moneycontrol |date=12 April 2023 |language=en |archive-date=15 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230415070158/https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/business/stocks/ongc-shares-as-investors-book-profits-after-sharp-gains-10399651.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In May 2023, ONGC announced that it would start its oil production in the [[Krishna Godavari Basin]] by June<ref>{{Cite web |last=Baruah |first=Rituraj |date=5 May 2023 |title=ONGC to start oil production in KG basin by June |url=https://www.livemint.com/companies/ongc-to-start-oil-production-in-kg-basin-by-june-11683304066806.html |access-date=6 May 2023 |website=mint |language=en |archive-date=5 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505185946/https://www.livemint.com/companies/ongc-to-start-oil-production-in-kg-basin-by-june-11683304066806.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and appointed Manish Patil as its director of human resources.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Anand |first=Saurav |date=5 May 2023 |title=ONGC appoints Manish Patil as director of human resources |url=https://www.livemint.com/companies/news/ongc-appoints-manish-patil-as-director-of-human-resources-11683303568014.html |access-date=6 May 2023 |website=mint |language=en |archive-date=5 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505180203/https://www.livemint.com/companies/news/ongc-appoints-manish-patil-as-director-of-human-resources-11683303568014.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Operations==
ONGC's operations include conventional exploration and production, refining and progressive development of alternative energy sources like coal-bed methane and shale gas.<ref name=CSR201112>{{cite web |url=http://www.ongcindia.com/wps/wcm/connect/1e263a3b-25a9-4e2f-a960-5e057f99ab09/GRI3.pdf?MOD=AJPERES&CACHEID=1e263a3b-25a9-4e2f-a960-5e057f99ab09 |title=Corporate Sustainability Report 2011-12 |publisher=ONGC |access-date=10 November 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109205134/http://www.ongcindia.com/wps/wcm/connect/1e263a3b-25a9-4e2f-a960-5e057f99ab09/GRI3.pdf?MOD=AJPERES&CACHEID=1e263a3b-25a9-4e2f-a960-5e057f99ab09 |archive-date=9 November 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref> The company's domestic operations are structured around 11 assets (predominantly oil and gas producing properties), 7 basins (exploratory properties), 2 plants (at [[Hazira Gas Processing Complex|Hazira]] and Uran) and services (for necessary inputs and support such as drilling, geo-physical, logging and well services).<ref name=CSR201112/>

===Subsidiaries===
ONGC Videsh Limited (OVL) is the international arm of ONGC. It was rechristened on 15 June 1989. The primary business of ONGC Videsh is to prospect for oil and gas acreages outside India, including exploration, development and production of oil and gas. It currently has 38 projects across 17 countries. Its oil and gas production reached 8.87 MMT of O+oEG in 2010, up from 0.252 MMT of O+OEG in 2002/03. ONGC holds 100% stake in ONGC Videsh Limited.<ref name=AR201213/>

[[Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited]] (HPCL) is an Indian state-owned [[petroleum|oil]] and [[natural gas]] company with its headquarters at [[Mumbai, Maharashtra]]. It has about 25% market-share in India among public-sector companies (PSUs) and a strong marketing infrastructure. Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited is an oil refinery at Mangalore. MRPL has a design capacity to process 15 million tonnes per annum and has two hydrocrackers producing premium diesel (high cetane). It also has 2 CCRs producing unleaded petrol of high octane.{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}}

ONGC Mangalore Petrochemicals Limited (OMPL) is an Indian company promoted by Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL). Both ONGC and MRPL hold respectively 49% and 51% stake in the company. OMPL is a subsidiary company of MRPL and also a PSU behalf of share pattern of OMPL. It was incorporated on 19 December 2006. The OMPL complex spans 442 acres of land in Mangalore Special Economic Zone (SEZ). The project cost was estimated at {{INRConvert|57.5|b}}. The complex is connected with MRPL Refinery, from where they feed to the complex is supplied. It is {{convert|14|km}} away from the New Mangalore Port and about {{convert|15|km}} from Mangalore International Airport.{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}}

====ONGC sports====
ONGC has held many sports teams, such as [[Sport of athletics|athletics]], [[badminton]], [[basketball]], [[boxing]], [[chess]], [[cricket]], [[cue sports]], [[carrom]], [[field hockey]], [[Association football|football]], [[kabaddi]], [[Shooting sport|shooting]], [[table tennis]], [[tennis]], [[volleyball]] and [[wrestling]]. Its football team, [[ONGC F.C.]], once played in Indian [[I-League]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}}

The basketball team, in particular, is known internationally since several of the players of [[India's national basketball team]] have played there. These players include [[Vishesh Bhriguvanshi]], [[Amritpal Singh (basketball)|Amritpal Singh]], and [[Yadwinder Singh]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}}

===Joint ventures===
====ONGC Tripura Power Company====
[[ONGC Tripura Power Company]] (OTPC) is a joint venture which was formed in September 2008 between ONGC, Infrastructure Leasing and Financial Services Limited and the [[government of Tripura]]. It has developed a 726.6 MW CCGT thermal power generation project at Palatana in [[Tripura]] which supply electricity to the power deficit areas of the northeastern states of the country.<ref>{{Cite web|title=We are the largest Natural Oil and Gas Company to Work in India|url=https://www.ongcindia.com/wps/wcm/connect/en/about-ongc/ongc-at-a-glance/corporate-profile/|access-date=25 February 2022|website=Ongcindia.com|archive-date=5 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220305090110/https://www.ongcindia.com/wps/wcm/connect/en/about-ongc/ongc-at-a-glance/corporate-profile/|url-status=live}}</ref> OTPC has 2 no 9FA machines supplied by [[General Electric|GE]] USA.{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}}

In the Brand Trust Report 2013, ONGC was ranked 191st among India's most trusted brands and subsequently, according to the Brand Trust Report 2014, ONGC was ranked 370th among India's most trusted brands.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.trustadvisory.info/allindia_2014.html |title=India's Most Trusted Brands 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150502221904/http://www.trustadvisory.info/allindia_2014.html |archive-date=2 May 2015 }}</ref>
* ONGC is the title sponsor for the first edition of the [[Corporate social responsibility]] (CSR) Award organised by Amar Ujala.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.amarujala.com/photo-gallery/india-news/amar-ujala-csr-award-in-presence-of-central-minister-piyush-goyal|title = Amar Ujala CSR Award|access-date = 31 October 2017|website = [[Amar Ujala]]|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171030181920/http://www.amarujala.com/photo-gallery/india-news/amar-ujala-csr-award-in-presence-of-central-minister-piyush-goyal|archive-date = 30 October 2017|url-status = live}}</ref>

==Controversies==
Despite being owned by the government of India, ONGC has repeatedly been found not claiming its rightful payments from private players, especially for the use of oil fields, oil rigs and concessions.<ref name="toi">{{cite news |title=CAG hauls up ONGC for giving oil rigs to RIL for free |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/CAG-hauls-up-ONGC-for-hiring-RIL-drilling-rig-without-bidding/articleshow/16249407.cms |access-date=31 October 2018 |publisher=Times of India |date=4 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120907214811/http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/CAG-hauls-up-ONGC-for-hiring-RIL-drilling-rig-without-bidding/articleshow/16249407.cms |archive-date=7 September 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref>

ONGC was owed {{INRConvert|920|b|mode=historical|year=2016}} from [[Reliance Industries Limited]] ([[Reliance Petroleum|Petrochemicals]]) for the use of blocks of oil fields. This was highlighted by the [[Comptroller and Auditor General of India]] (CAG), the overseer of expenditures of the Indian Government. However, as of 2018, this outstanding amount was still not paid by Reliance Industries Limited to ONGC.<ref>{{cite web |title=Auditors report |url=https://tenders.ongc.co.in/wps/wcm/reportspdf/common/auditors08.pdf |website=Tenders.ongc.co.in |publisher=ONGC |access-date=31 October 2018 }}{{Dead link|date=April 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

On 21 April 2021, three employees (Mohini Mohan Gogoi, Alakesh Saikia, Retul Saikia) of the ONGC were allegedly abducted from Lakuwa field of [[Sivasagar district|Assam's Sivasagar district]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=21 April 2021|title=Three ONGC employees 'abducted' in Assam, ULFA-I suspected|url=https://indianexpress.com/article/india/ongc-employees-abducted-assam-7282475/|access-date=21 April 2021|website=The Indian Express|language=en|archive-date=21 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421035441/https://indianexpress.com/article/india/ongc-employees-abducted-assam-7282475/|url-status=live}}</ref> Authorities suspect that the banned [[United Liberation Front of Asom|United Liberation Front of Asom (Independent)]] is behind the abduction.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Ulfa abducts 3 ONGC personnel from Assam's Charaideo district – Times of India|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/ulfa-abducts-3-ongc-personnel-in-assams-charaideo-district/articleshow/82172941.cms|access-date=21 April 2021|website=The Times of India|date=21 April 2021|language=en|archive-date=21 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421031827/http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/ulfa-abducts-3-ongc-personnel-in-assams-charaideo-district/articleshow/82172941.cms|url-status=live}}</ref>

Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) has faced criticism for maintaining business operations in Russia despite international sanctions imposed following [[Russian invasion of Ukraine|Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022]]. The company continued to sell Russian Sokol crude oil to Indian refiners, drawing concerns over its role in supporting Russia's energy sector. ONGC has been listed on platforms like ''Leave Russia'', which tracks companies still engaged in the Russian market, raising questions about its alignment with global economic sanctions and ethical considerations.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-03-29 |title='ONGC sells Russia's Sokol oil to Indian refiners' |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/ongc-sells-russias-sokol-oil-to-indian-refiners/articleshow/90504107.cms |access-date=2025-01-29 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=ONGC |url=https://leave-russia.org/ongc |access-date=2025-01-29 |website=leave-russia.org |language=en}}</ref>

extract:
The Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC) is an Indian central public sector undertaking which is the largest government-owned oil and gas explorer and producer in the country. It accounts for around 70 per cent of India's domestic production of crude oil and around 84 per cent of natural gas. Headquartered in Delhi, ONGC is under the ownership of the Government of India and administration of Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. It was founded on 14 August 1956 by the Government of India. In November 2010, the Government of India conferred the Maharatna status to ONGC.
In a survey by the Government of India for fiscal year 2019–20, it was ranked as the largest profit making central public sector undertaking (PSU) in India. It is ranked 5th among the Top 250 Global Energy Companies by Platts.
ONGC is vertically integrated across the entire oil and gas industry. It is involved in exploring for and exploiting hydrocarbons in 26 sedimentary basins of India, owns and operates over 11,000 kilometers of pipelines in the country and operates a total of around 230 drilling and workover rigs. Its international subsidiary ONGC Videsh currently has projects in 15 countries. ONGC has discovered seven out of the eight producing Indian basins, adding over 7.15 billion tonnes of In-place Oil & Gas volume of hydrocarbons in Indian basins. Against a global decline of production from matured fields, ONGC has maintained production from its brownfields like Mumbai High, with the help of aggressive investments in various IOR (improved oil recovery) and EOR (Enhanced Oil Recovery) schemes. ONGC has many matured fields with a current recovery factor of 25–33%. Its Reserve Replacement Ratio for between 2005 and 2013, has been more than one.
During FY 2012–13, ONGC had to share the highest ever under-recovery of ₹89.77 trillion (US$1.53 trillion) (an increase of ₹17.89 billion (US$305.3 million) over the previous financial year) towards the under-recoveries of Oil Marketing Companies (IOC, BPCL and HPCL).
On 1 November 2017, the Union Cabinet approved ONGC for acquiring a majority 51.11% stake in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL). On 30 January 2018, ONGC completed the acquisition of 51.11% stake in HPCL.
